# Is Muscle Linked to Longevity?

How much muscle you have, and how strong those muscles are, can predict how long you’ll live.

Your muscles make and release important proteins, and play a role in glucose metabolism.

In this blog post:

- muscle and longevity links
- how to measure muscle mass
- how to build muscle
- retaining muscle on [GLP-1s](https://immortals.com/collections/weight-loss-prescriptions)

## Why is muscle linked to longevity?

From age 30, you lose ~3-5% of your muscle mass per decade. That rate accelerates after 60. With less muscle, you gradually become weaker, less independent, and more likely to fall.

But that’s not the only reason that less muscle = worse health.

Skeletal muscle is the largest site of glucose disposal in the body. For example, 80% of the glucose your body clears after a meal is taken up by muscle tissue.

More healthy muscle gives your body greater capacity to clear glucose, which:

- supports insulin sensitivity
- helps maintain healthy blood sugar levels
- may reduce your risk of prediabetes

Your muscles are also in constant conversation with the rest of your body, working as endocrine organs.

When you contract a muscle, it releases signaling proteins called myokines. Myokines carry messages to organs like your brain, gut, liver, and skin.

Myokines influence:

- cognition
- lipid metabolism
- bone formation
- skin structure
- blood vessel function
- body weight regulation
- inflammation
- tumor growth

And it’s not just how much muscle you have… Muscle strength plays a role in longevity, too.

Grip strength, often used as a proxy for overall muscle strength, is inversely associated with markers of biological aging. (Stronger grip is linked to slower biological aging.) It can also be a better predictor of all-cause mortality than systolic blood pressure.

The effects aren’t small.

A [2026 study](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2845052) on ~5,500 older women found those in the strongest quarter for grip strength had a 30% lower risk of death from any cause compared to those in the weakest quarter.

This accounted for physical activity and sedentary time, suggesting the link isn’t just general exercise.

## How to measure muscle mass

More precise ways to measure muscle mass use imaging tests such as:

- DEXA scans
- MRIs
- CT scans

You can also use smart scales to measure and track your muscle mass at home.

For example, [Withings BodyScan 2](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/withings-bodyscan-2) measures muscle and fat mass. It analyzes your arms, legs, and torso separately, so you can track where you’re gaining or losing muscle. Fat-mass measurements correlate ≥99% with clinical DEXA in internal testing.

For grip strength, you can test yours with a hand dynamometer. They cost ~$20.

Here’s what to aim for per age group.

## How to build muscle

### #1. Strength train

Strength training loads your muscles more than they’re used to. Your body responds to this strain by rebuilding muscles bigger and stronger.

Tips:

- aim for 2-3 strength training sessions per week.
- gradually increase the stimulus by lifting heavier weights or doing more reps. (This is known as progressive overload.)
- stop 1-3 reps short of failure. Pooled data from [15 studies](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9935748/) found no evidence that grinding out that last rep builds more muscle.

### #2. Eat enough protein

Your body uses protein to repair and build muscle.

Most people trying to maintain or build muscle should aim for 1.2-1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day. To build muscle, aim toward the upper end of that range.

Get protein from:

- eggs
- nuts and seeds
- lean chicken and turkey breast
- legumes, like chickpeas, lentils, and beans
- clean [protein powders](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/longevity-protein-chocolate)

### #3. Take creatine

Creatine helps your muscles regenerate energy during short, hard efforts. That lets you do a little more work each session, promoting more muscle gain.

[Creatine](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/creatine) supports:*

- muscle function
- muscle growth
- strength
- recovery between training sessions

### #4. Get enough sleep

Missing out on sleep can interfere with muscle growth.

In a small study, acute sleep deprivation reduced muscle protein synthesis (the process of repairing and growing muscle) by 18%.

Tips:

- aim for 7-9 hours of sleep a night.
- avoid food 4+ hours before bed.
- create a calming 60-min wind-down routine.
- get light in eyes first thing to anchor your circadian rhythm.

### #5. Consider prescription support for growth hormone production

Growth hormone declines ~15% every decade after 30. This hormone plays an important role in metabolism and muscle health.

[Sermorelin](https://immortals.com/products/sermorelin) is a peptide that prompts your body to release its own growth hormone. This may support muscle gain, as well as fat loss, sleep, and recovery.

You can access doctor-trusted peptides through [Immortals Medicine](https://immortals.com/pages/immortals-medicine).**

## How to preserve muscle on a GLP-1

If you’re on a [GLP-1](https://immortals.com/collections/weight-loss-prescriptions), it’s even more important to keep an eye on your muscle mass.

Any weight loss comes with the risk of losing some muscle alongside fat. GLP-1-based weight loss can also include lean mass loss, so preserving muscle is important. Plus, with a lowered appetite, it’s harder to get in enough protein to feed those muscles.

Tips:

- **protein first:** Prioritize protein at the start of your meal, so you get enough in before you become full.
- **snacks and shakes:** If your appetite is really low, go for small meals, [protein shakes](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/metabolic-protein-powder), or high-protein snacks (like hard-boiled eggs, unsweetened yogurt, nuts, legumes, and [protein bars](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/macadamia-protein-bar)).
- **strength train:** Strength train throughout GLP-1 treatment… and beyond. Make 2-3 sessions a week a habit, and work all muscle groups, including legs, arms, core, and back.
- **glycine:** Consider a [compounded GLP-1 with glycine](https://immortals.com/products/tirzepatide?variant=50231113744623), if prescribed. Glycine may support muscle health during weight loss.

Muscle mass is a biomarker of aging. Make building and maintaining it part of your longevity protocol.

# Vaginal Microbiome Test Launch

Every day, I test my vaginal microbiome.

It's part of my $2.6M experiment to better understand female health… and I think the vaginal microbiome is one of the most overlooked datasets in a woman's body.

So today, we are launching our first women’s-specific test:

## Why I measure mine

Your vagina has a microbiome… and it’s unlike any other in your body.

In the gut, diversity is healthy. In the vagina, it’s the warning sign. A healthy vagina is dominated by a single bacteria… Lactobacillus crispatus… which keeps the environment acidic and stops harmful bacteria from growing.

An in-balance microbiome is protective.

But when out of balance, it’s linked to…

- higher rates of preterm birth
- higher risk of acquiring HIV
- lower IVF success
- higher risk of catching other STIs
- higher risk of miscarriage
- higher risk of pelvic inflammatory disease

Most imbalances are asymptomatic, so a lot of women are in that state without knowing.

Fortunately, the vaginal microbiome is one of the most responsive systems in the body. It changes within days of a behavior change.

## What the test shows

Most tests check for a handful of organisms…. this one reads the DNA in your sample. It then identifies everything it finds for 10,000+ organisms.

You’ll see:

- if you’re L crispatus dominant
- bacterial and fungal load
- microbiome balance
- breakdown of every organism found
- results for 4 common STIs

A board-certified physician writes and reviews every result.

It's an at-home kit. You swab for 20 seconds, put your sample in the prepaid return bag, and send it off.

Your results arrive in a secure dashboard in 4-9 business days.

If you want to talk through them, you can book time with a doctor trained in microbiome analysis for an extra charge.* They can prescribe treatment if it's appropriate.

I test every day, but you do not need to. The reason I am testing so frequently is to track how my microbiome changes across my menstrual cycle. We’re comparing these results with 1,900 biomarkers in a world-first experiment.

You can test once to understand your baseline.

If you then want to improve your results, you can try interventions and test again to see how your microbiome changes across time. Every 3 months is plenty to check how a specific change (alcohol, a new partner, antibiotics) actually affected you.

# Bryan Johnson's Social Media Fast

I’ve cut my social media use by 50% and I feel 100% better.

I recently did a 7-day social media fast. It felt like the most effective longevity therapy I’ve done.

Everything got better:

- mood
- sleep
- energy
- presence
- judgment
- relationships
- optimism
- [exercise performance](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/blogs/news/exercise-and-fitness-protocol-for-longevity)
- mental clarity

Evidence shows a [7-day fast](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645342/) produces a reduction in anxiety (16%), depression (25%), and insomnia (15%).

The effects felt bigger.

Conversely, dipping back in, I can viscerally feel that my body metabolizes social media similarly to a fast-food meal, corrosive relationship, hangover, and sleep deprivation. My body hates it.

## The protocol

I abstained from all social media for 7 days.

That meant no:

- Instagram
- X
- TikTok
- Facebook
- YouTube

I could listen to:

- audiobooks
- podcasts

I’ve previously done 40-hour and 70-hour social media fasts. Same rules.

## What I learned

Day 1 was awkward in the first few minutes. I didn’t know what to do with myself. Once I settled in, it was a kid-like experience. Unstructured, open play with no expectations from the world.

I noticed more things around me. I noticed more of my own thoughts. More of my emotions.

By day 7, I never wanted to be on social media again.

After the previous fasts, I wrote that social media is pollution. Not a vice or guilty pleasure. It’s closer to water toxins, air pollution, and microplastics.

This time, the major insight was that social media is a form of intoxication.

Alcohol is honest intoxication. It clearly tells you what it’s taking from you. Social media, on the other hand, does not disclose itself as an intoxicant.

It produces the sensation of being informed, engaged, and connected while quietly evacuating your capacity for depth and independent thought.

You don’t feel drunk. You feel current. But [evidence](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10216498/) shows that it causes your brain to shrink. The impairment is real, but you can’t feel it. Making it the more dangerous type.

Until I took a break, I was unaware of how much cognitive space social media was occupying.

The vast majority of social media is junk food. The timeline and comments are flooded with rage, meanness, and slop. Terribly unhealthy for anyone.

It makes me grateful for the few voices who are genuinely positive and constructive in their presence.

## What you can do

If you haven’t tried it, I encourage you to try a social media fast. Even if for one day.

Tips:

- replace social media time with something valuable to you: outside activities, new hobbies, quiet time, reading, exercise, time with friends, sleep.
- notice how you feel.

# Does Bryan Johnson Drink Coffee?

Coffee is one of the most studied longevity drinks in the world… and I don’t drink it.

I personally find caffeine destabilizes my mood, disrupts my sleep, stains my teeth, and creates too much of a metabolic rollercoaster for me.

I will occasionally drink decaf.

However, coffee may be a perfect fit for you.

In this blog post:

- coffee’s longevity link
- decaf vs. caffeinated
- my decaf protocol
- what you should do

## Coffee longevity link

Drinking coffee is linked to living nearly 2 additional years of healthy life.

It can support:

- lung health
- metabolic health
- heart health
- memory
- mood
- healthy aging

Why? It’s not just the caffeine. Coffee contains more than 2,000 compounds, including bioactive compounds such as melanoidins and chlorogenic acids.

Melanoidins have antioxidant properties, along with anti-inflammatory and anti-hypertensive (blood-pressure-lowering) effects.

Chlorogenic acids are a type of polyphenol, plant-based compounds found in fruits, vegetables, and [olive oil](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/extra-virgin-olive-oil). They also have antioxidant properties and may help promote a healthy inflammatory response, healthy immune function, and metabolic resilience.

And the most famous compound, caffeine, has many of its own health benefits, including potentially influencing apoptosis (in laboratory studies). This process helps rid your body of damaged cells.

Coffee may also support longevity by:

- protecting neurons
- promoting vascular function and blood flow
- boosting metabolic rate
- inducing autophagy (shown mainly in animal studies), which is the body’s cellular recycling system

## Coffee timing matters for longevity

Compared to non-coffee drinkers, morning-only coffee drinkers have a:

- 16% lower risk of death from any cause
- 31% lower risk of cardiovascular death

In that study, all-day coffee drinkers did not show the same mortality benefit.

**Why timing matters:** The half-life of caffeine in blood is ~5-6 hours. A cup at 4 p.m. leaves about half of that caffeine in your system at 10 p.m. when you’re trying to sleep.

Beyond sleep loss, drinking coffee later in the day might decrease melatonin levels and disrupt circadian rhythms, which may affect oxidative stress, blood pressure, and cardiovascular disease risk.

## Does decaf make a difference?

Most of coffee’s longevity benefits show up in decaf, too.

Decaf still contains chlorogenic acids, melanoidins, and other compounds that may contribute to these benefits.

Just like caffeinated coffee, decaf is associated with heart and metabolic health benefits. Several large studies suggest decaf may have similar associations with lower mortality as caffeinated coffee.

## My coffee protocol

I occasionally have decaf coffee with macadamia nut milk with breakfast.

Breakfast usually includes veggies, legumes, and [extra virgin olive oil](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/extra-virgin-olive-oil).

In the morning, I also have:

- [Longevity Mix](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/collections/longevity-mix)
- [Creatine](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/creatine)
- [Longevity Protein](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/longevity-protein-chocolate) mixed with [Blueberry Nut Mix](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/nutty-pudding-fruit-and-nut-mix), [Collagen Peptides](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/collagen), [Extra Virgin Olive Oil](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/extra-virgin-olive-oil), and berries
- [Essential Capsules](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/essentials-capsules)
- [Advanced Antioxidants](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/advanced-antioxidants)
- [Ashwagandha + Rhodiola](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/ashwagandha-rhodiola-120mg)
- [Omega-3](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/omega-3)
- NMN

## What you should do

If you like it, drink coffee for the health benefits. That could be decaf or caffeinated, depending on your preference and tolerance.

Tips:

- **timing:** If you drink caffeinated coffee, drink it early. We recommend avoiding caffeine at least 8-10 hours before bed to avoid wrecking sleep.
- **moderation:** Most longevity benefits are seen at 1-4 cups a day. Beyond that, there may be little additional benefit.
- **additions:** Avoid sugar, flavored syrups, and cream. Go for black coffee or add milk or nut milk.
- **decaf:** Track your sleep. If caffeinated coffee disrupts it, switch to decaf. You’ll still get many health benefits. Protecting sleep is your #1 priority.

# Bryan Johnson's Longevity Bowl Recipe

Bryan has this longevity bowl on repeat, along with [Super Veggie](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/blogs/news/how-to-make-my-anti-aging-lunch-live-to-120) and [Nutty Pudding](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/blogs/news/bryan-johnsons-nutty-pudding-recipe).

The recipe combines leafy greens, cruciferous vegetables, legumes, and antioxidant-rich herbs and spices for broad nutrient coverage.

Here's how to make it if you want to try eating like Bryan.

## Ingredients (1–2 servings)

- 1 Japanese sweet potato
- ½ bunch of asparagus
- 5–6 kale leaves
- 1 red bell pepper
- 2 carrots
- ¼ cup walnuts
- handful of cilantro
- ½ tsp [extra virgin olive oil](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/extra-virgin-olive-oil)
- Handful of green onions
- 1 lemon
- handful of chopped dill
- ½ cup white beans
- 1 tbsp apple cider vinegar
- ½ tsp cumin seeds

## Nutritional info (per serving)

- calories: ~390
- carbs: ~61 grams
- protein: ~14 grams
- fat: ~13 grams
- fiber: ~17 grams

## Instructions

1. Poke a few holes in the sweet potato and lightly cover with [extra virgin olive oil](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/extra-virgin-olive-oil).
2. Roast the sweet potato for 45–60 minutes at 400°F (~200°C).
3. Roast the red pepper for 25–30 minutes at 400°F (~200°C). Thinly slice after roasting.
4. Trim off and discard the woody ends of the asparagus. Place the remaining asparagus in a large skillet with 1 inch of water and boil for 2–5 minutes.
5. Rinse and drain the white beans. Top with the juice of 1 lemon and a handful of chopped dill.
6. Shred the carrots and massage with apple cider vinegar and cumin seeds.
7. Chop the kale, add a splash of olive oil, and massage with your hands until the kale softens.
8. Assemble the bowl with sweet potato, asparagus, red pepper, bean salad, kale, and shredded carrots.
9. Top with toasted walnuts, green onion, cilantro, and a squeeze of lemon juice.

You can also explore Blueprint [nutrition](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/collections/nutrition) to see what else Bryan has in rotation right now.

Nutritional information is an estimate and may vary depending on the specific brands and ingredients used.

# Is Vitamin D Good for Longevity?

Vitamin D supports your bones, immune system, and blood pressure regulation… and yet [~77% of people](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2023.1070808/full) don’t get enough.*

Supplementing can help protect the life of telomeres, which are an important factor in healthy aging.*

In this blog post:

- what is vitamin D
- longevity link
- where to get it (and why the sun isn’t the best place)

## What is vitamin D?

Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin that regulates the function of more than 200 genes.

There are two forms, D2 and D3, both of which are converted into 25-hydroxyvitamin D in the liver, and then into 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D in the kidneys.

1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, the biologically active form of vitamin D, is involved in:

- cell growth
- bone formation
- immune function
- insulin production
- blood pressure regulation
- and more*

## Is vitamin D good for longevity?

Getting enough vitamin D does a lot for your body.

For example…

### Bones

Vitamin D is needed for bone growth and remodeling, and it helps your body absorb calcium, another important nutrient for bone health.

Supplementing vitamin D helps support strong bones as you age.*

### Immune function

Vitamin D helps maintain a healthy immune system.*

It may also enhance autophagy, which is when your body breaks down and recycles old cell parts.*

### Aging

[Research](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40409468/) also shows that vitamin D3 supplements can extend the time it takes to shorten telomeres, effectively promoting healthy aging.*

This study involved taking 2,000 IU vitamin D3 over 4 years. Longevity is a long game.

## How much vitamin D do you need?

The recommended dietary allowance for vitamin D is 600 IU for men and women. This bumps up to 800 IU for those over 70.

Research on supplementation is mixed. Many studies look at 2,000 IU. Bryan takes 2,000 IU of vitamin D daily.

## Where to get vitamin D

You have a few options.

### Food

Vitamin D is found in foods like:

- egg yolks
- cheese
- mushrooms
- fatty fish (e.g., trout, salmon, and mackerel)
- fortified foods (e.g., milk or cereal)

Eating these foods can help you top up levels… but it’s difficult to get enough vitamin D through food alone.

### Sunlight

Your body makes vitamin D from sunlight. This needs to be direct sunlight. Not sunlight through a window. Not sunlight through sunscreen.

It’s unclear how much you need. Some researchers suggest spending 15–20 min a day in sunlight with 40% of your skin exposed. Depending on where you live, this might not be possible all year round.

That’s not the only problem. People with darker skin tones and older adults don’t produce as much vitamin D from sunlight. And as sun exposure can cause [skin aging](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/collections/skincare) and skin cancer, supplements can be a safer source.

See [Bryan’s sunlight protocol here](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/blogs/news/why-i-avoid-the-sun).

### Supplements

You can find vitamin D2 and vitamin D3 supplements. Both increase your 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels. But vitamin D3 increases them more and maintains higher levels for longer.*

You can find dedicated vitamin D supplements or multivitamins that cover more needs in one protocol.

For example, [Essential Capsules](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/essentials-capsules) contain 2,000 IU vitamin D3 along with 22 other longevity actives.

Whatever you decide, make sure you’re getting enough vitamin D, and consider supplements over too much sun exposure as your source.

# 4 Protocols to Follow After 40

Bryan Johnson ran his body down for years… then rebuilt it in his 40s.

That decade is a bigger deal than most people realize.

Researchers tracking thousands of molecules found the first major aging burst happens around [age 44](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43587-024-00692-2). Molecules related to cardiovascular disease, skin and muscle aging, and lipid metabolism shift in both men and women.

Aging doesn't happen gradually. It happens in bursts.

Bryan is proof it's never too late to turn things around.

Here are 4 protocols to follow after 40 to fight back against the "burst."

## #1. Strength train to fight muscle and bone density loss

In your 30s and 40s, you begin losing muscle mass (a process called sarcopenia) and [bone density](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/blogs/news/bone-health-protocol).

For muscle, you lose ~3-5% every 10 years, with an accelerating aging burst in your mid-40s.

For bone, you reach peak bone density between ages 25-30, and it declines from there. The bone density drop is even steeper for women during menopause, which happens around age 50.

You might not notice muscle and bone density loss, but it compounds over time.

Muscle strength is among the best predictors of how well you age. Grip strength, for example, is potentially a stronger predictor of all-cause and [cardiovascular mortality](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(14)62000-6/abstract) than systolic blood pressure. And bone density is the difference between a stumble in your 70s and a life-altering fracture.

Strength training is one of the few protocols that defends both at once. Resistance exercises provide mechanical load, or stress, to your bones. Your bones adapt to this stress by getting stronger, increasing density in response to resistance.

The protocol:

- **strength train 2-3 times a week:** If you're new, start with bodyweight exercises or work with a trainer.
- **work all major muscle groups:** Do compound movements, including squats, lunges, rows, presses, and deadlifts.
- **do progressive overload:** Gradually lift heavier weights or do more reps over time.
- **eat enough protein for muscle repair:** Eat 1.2-1.6 grams of [protein](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/collections/protein) per kilogram of body weight. Women should increase this to 2 grams in the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle, during perimenopause, and after menopause.

## #2. Track biomarkers more closely

In your 40s, several biomarkers related to long-term health start drifting up.

For example, arteries tend to stiffen and cells grow more resistant to insulin with age. This shows up in your biomarkers as elevated blood pressure and blood glucose.

If you know your numbers and check them on a schedule, you can act early when changes are easier to reverse.

Key numbers to keep an eye on:

- blood pressure
- cholesterol
- blood sugar
- apolipoprotein B (ApoB, a key marker of heart health)

You can track 100+ important numbers with [Biomarkers](https://immortals.com/pages/biomarkers).

Beyond biomarker measurement, get more regular health checks from your 40s onward, including:

- **eye exams** every 2-4 years from age 40-54, then more regularly
- **colorectal cancer screenings** starting from age 45 (some stool and blood tests should be annual, while colonoscopies are every 10 years, or 5 years with a family history of colon cancer)
- for women, **breast cancer screenings** every 1-2 years from age 40 to 74

A healthcare provider can let you know if you'd benefit from any other screenings and the ideal schedule to follow.

## #3. Ramp up skin and haircare protocols

Your 40s are when 2 decades of slow change start to show up in the mirror.

**Skin:** Natural collagen production drops by ~1% each year after age 25. This is the protein that keeps skin firm and elastic. Accumulated sun damage may also start to show up in your 40s as dark spots, sagging, and wrinkles.

**Hair:** By age 20, ~20% of men already have some visible hair loss. By 50, 40% of women will have visible hair loss. But many people lose up to 50% of their hair before they start to notice thinning. Grays start to set in, too.

The protocol:

- **reverse hair loss:** Consider treatments like [oral minoxidil](https://medicine.immortals.com/treatments/minoxidil), topical minoxidil, finasteride, and/or [low-level laser light therapy](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/laser-cap) (LLLT).
- **protect aging hair:** Use peptide haircare (like [Blueprint Peptide Hair Serum and Shampoo](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/collections/haircare)) to support the appearance of stronger, healthier-looking hair.
- **reverse skin damage:** [Tretinoin](https://medicine.immortals.com/treatments/tretinoin) stimulates collagen production, improves skin texture and fine lines, and reverses photoaging. Protect your skin when the UV index is >4 to minimize future sun damage.
- **protect aging skin:** The [Blueprint Skincare Stack](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/collections/skincare) contains SFC and NMN, which help reduce visible signs of aging and support natural collagen production. Supplement with [Collagen Peptides](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/collagen) daily.

## #4. Take sleep hygiene more seriously

You can't run on bad sleep like you did when you were 23… you shouldn't even do that at 23.

Sleep is vital for healthy aging, but it also seems to get more difficult with age. Deep sleep declines, hormonal changes cause more fragmented sleep, and your circadian rhythm becomes less robust.

Paying more attention to sleep hygiene (the habits that help sleep) can help you continue to get enough of it.

[Sleep tips](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/blogs/news/10-habits-for-sleep):

- **keep a consistent schedule:** Anchor your circadian rhythm by going to bed at the same time (+/- 30 min) each night and getting morning light within 15-30 min of waking.
- **avoid eating close to bedtime:** Start by avoiding food 1-2 hours before bed and move back from there. Aim for at least 4 hours.
- **stay cool:** Keep your bedroom temperature between 60-67°F (15-19°C) and use breathable bedding or a [cooling mattress](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/eight-sleep). This is even more important for women during perimenopause, which can start in your 40s and cause night sweats.
- **monitor for sleep apnea:** Loud snoring, gasping, and daytime exhaustion are worth raising with a doctor. Sleep apnea undermines your sleep, no matter how good your sleep hygiene is. It's more common with age, but treatable.

Remember, the first aging burst hits around age 44… but it's not the point of no return. It's a cue to dial in your protocols while changes are easier to defend against.

# 14 Brain Health Protocols

Up to [45% of dementia cases](https://www.alzint.org/about/risk-factors-risk-reduction/) could be prevented or delayed.

Genetics and aging play a role… there are also [14 modifiable risk factors](https://www.emro.who.int/media/news/alzheimers-and-brain-awareness-month.html). Your habits today shape your brain health decades from now. Here are the 14 risk factors and brain health protocols for each.

## #1. Physical inactivity

Exercise may help prevent dementia through mechanisms like increased blood flow and decreased production of beta-amyloid, a protein linked to dementia when it builds up.

**What to do:**

- aim for 150 min of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75 min of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity a week.
- increase this to 6 hours a week if you can.

## #2. Excessive alcohol consumption

Excessive alcohol consumption is linked to reduced brain volume and signs of brain damage. Drinking more than 12 drinks a week may increase dementia risk.

**What to do:**

- Bryan avoids alcohol entirely.
- start with limiting alcohol to 12 drinks or less/week.

## #3. Air pollution

PM2.5 (fine particles with a diameter of 2.5 micrometers or less) and PM10 (10 micrometers or less) can cause brain inflammation and increase dementia risk.

**What to do:**

- **monitor air quality in your home:** Look for a monitor labeled for indoor use. Place it in a typical breathing zone (e.g., not right up against a wall or near a gas stove or open window). A monitor can help you judge if you need to increase ventilation or minimize gas stove use.
- **improve indoor quality:** Get a HEPA air purifier and let it run in your bedroom overnight. Upgrade your HVAC filter to MERV 13 if your system supports it and clean or replace your filter regularly.
- **monitor outdoor air quality:** Use [AirNow.gov](https://www.airnow.gov/) or your weather app. Reduce long or intense outdoor exercise when the air quality index (AQI) is above 150.

## #4. Smoking

Smoking can cause oxidative stress and damage the brain. It's also linked to cognitive degeneration, including volume loss.

**What to do:**

- if you smoke, get help quitting.
- if you don't smoke, don't start.

## #5. Limited social contact

Social isolation can lead to less cognitive stimulation, more brain inflammation, and impaired cognitive functioning.

**What to do:**

- join clubs and social communities.
- prioritize time with friends and family. Set up recurring plans to put connection on autopilot.
- aim for 1 meaningful conversation a day.
- treat your social life like the important longevity protocol it is.

## #6. High cholesterol levels

High levels of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, aka "bad cholesterol," is one of the largest modifiable risk factors for dementia.

**What to do:**

- get 7-9 hours of sleep.
- exercise regularly.
- eat a heart-healthy diet (fruits, veggies, whole grains, [extra virgin olive oil](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/extra-virgin-olive-oil), etc.)
- test cholesterol levels regularly. (You can do this with [Biomarkers](https://immortals.com/pages/biomarkers)).
- get a prescription for cholesterol-lowering medications if needed.

## #7. Obesity

Obesity can contribute to chronic inflammation, which can damage white matter in the brain.

**What to do:**

- manage weight through nutrition, exercise, [sleep](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/blogs/news/10-habits-for-sleep), and stress management.
- work toward a healthy weight range if needed. Aim for a waist-to-height ratio of 0.5 or lower. Divide your waist circumference in inches by your height in inches to find your waist-to-height ratio.
- consider medications for weight management if helpful.

## #8. High blood pressure

High blood pressure can cause oxidative stress, brain shrinkage, reduced clearance of beta-amyloid, and more.

Medication for high blood pressure is the only known effective preventative medication for dementia.

**What to do:**

- monitor blood pressure regularly (aim to maintain systolic blood pressure of 120 mmHg or less from age 40).
- eat a healthy diet, exercise, and get enough sleep.
- take blood pressure medication if needed.

## #9. Hearing loss

Less auditory input leads to less stimulation. Hearing loss coincides with 30-40% faster brain shrinkage and increases your risk of dementia up to 5x.

**What to do:**

- download a decibel app like the [Decibel X app](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/decibel-x-db-sound-level-meter/id448155923).
- protect your ears at 80 decibels or higher.
- wear custom-molded earplugs in loud environments.
- get hearing aids as soon as you need them.

You can learn about [Bryan's hearing protection protocol](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/blogs/news/hearing-protection-protocol) here.

## #10. Vision loss

Eye conditions like cataracts and diabetic retinopathy can increase dementia risk. In some cases, treatment reverses the risk.

**What to do:**

- get an eye exam every 2-4 years, and more often with age.
- address treatable eye conditions.

## #11. Depression

Depression is one of the earliest symptoms of dementia. It's unclear if depression causes dementia or if it's the other way around.

**What to do:**

- watch out for symptoms of depression, like persistent sadness, hopelessness, and appetite changes.
- get treatment if you experience it. E.g., therapy, antidepressants, brain stimulation.

## #12. Diabetes

High blood sugar may lead to inflammation in the brain and a loss of neurons.

**What to do:**

- monitor blood sugar and diabetes risk with [HbA1C tests](https://immortals.com/pages/biomarkers).
- eat a healthy diet and exercise regularly to control blood sugar.

## #13. Head injury

This includes head injuries from falls, sports, and vehicle and bicycle accidents. Take precautions to reduce your risk.

**What to do:**

- wear a helmet when cycling or if your job requires it.
- wear protective equipment when playing contact sports.
- reduce fall risk by reducing clutter, loose rugs, etc., in the home. Especially important with age.

## #14. Mental stimulation

A low level of early-life brain stimulation affects cognitive reserve, or how well your brain can adapt and improvise.

More cognitive reserve = fewer cognitive decline symptoms. Some people have brain changes consistent with advanced Alzheimer's disease, but don't show any symptoms thanks to strong reserves.

You can't change early-life stimulation… but you can build cognitive reserve now with mentally stimulating activities, like puzzles, reading, and playing an instrument.

That was a lot. You don't need to address all 14 at once. Pick 1 brain health protocol to work on this week. Then pick another.

- 100% pure cocoa
- undutched
- third-party tested for heavy metals
- significant flavonoid content

# 6 Eye Health Protocols

Vision is the sense people are most afraid of losing… but hardly anyone knows there are protocols to keep your eye health sharp.

Part of the problem is that the standard advice (wear sunglasses, eat carrots) is too vague to act on. And the highest-impact protocols for long-term eye health are rarely framed as eye protocols at all.

Here are 6 things the evidence supports doing to protect your vision.

## #1. Exercise

Exercise helps almost every organ in your body. Eyes included.

One [study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6193839/) found that people who met baseline exercise guidelines (~150 min of moderate activity/week) had a 47% lower risk of developing glaucoma, the second leading cause of blindness worldwide.

Exercise lowers intraocular pressure. This is the fluid pressure inside your eye and the number 1 modifiable risk factor for glaucoma.

Aerobic exercise also appears to protect against age-related macular degeneration (AMD), which causes blurred vision and loss of central vision.

A [15-year study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1857544/) found people who exercised at least 3 times a week were 70% less likely to develop one type of AMD.

## #2. Wear proper UV-protective sunglasses

Sun exposure is a risk factor for:

- cataracts
- AMD
- eye cancer
- eye growths

The fix isn't to just wear sunglasses.

Bad sunglasses may be worse for your eyes than not wearing sunglasses at all. Dark lenses dilate your pupils and stop you from squinting, allowing more UV light to reach ocular tissues.

The real fix: Get sunglasses that provide UV400 or 100% UV protection.

## #3. Eat for the eyes

Prioritize lutein, zeaxanthin, and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA).

Lutein and zeaxanthin are types of carotenoids, or natural yellow-orange pigments.

They:

- support retinal health and visual clarity*
- are found in [Advanced Antioxidants](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/advanced-antioxidants), corn, eggs, salmon, kale, spinach, yellow and orange bell peppers, and carrots (there's some truth to that carrot advice)

DHA is a [type of omega-3 fatty acid](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/blogs/news/why-your-body-loves-omega-3) and the main fatty acid in the retina. It:

- supports clear vision and long-term eye health*
- is found in fatty fish (like salmon, sardines, and mackerel) and in [omega-3 supplements](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/omega-3)

## #4. Get regular eye exams

Glaucoma, AMD, and diabetic retinopathy (an eye disease linked to diabetes) are largely asymptomatic until they've already done damage.

Eye exams can catch them when they're still treatable.

Here's an eye exam schedule from the American Academy of Ophthalmology's [2026 guidelines](https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/comprehensive-adult-medical-eye-evaluation-ppp) for adults with no known risk factors:

- **under 40:** every 5-10 years
- **age 40-54:** every 2-4 years
- **age 55-64:** every 1-3 years
- **age 65+:** every 1-2 years

People with diabetes and those with a family history of glaucoma should screen more often than the baseline schedule.

## #5. Improve cardiovascular health

The same systems that protect your heart (controlled blood pressure, stable blood sugar, healthy lipids) protect your vision.

Hypertension, diabetes, and high cholesterol can damage blood vessels in the retina, cause blurry vision and macular degeneration, and contribute to cataracts and glaucoma.

Longevity interventions stack. Nothing you do for your cardiovascular system is wasted on your eyes.

Follow [heart-healthy protocols](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/blogs/news/4-heart-health-protocols) like:

- eating whole foods, including fruits, veggies, legumes, lean proteins, and whole grains
- exercising for at least 150 min (work your way up to 6 hours a week)
- getting 7-9 hours of sleep
- monitoring [biomarkers](https://immortals.com/pages/biomarkers) like blood pressure, HbA1c, and cholesterol, and taking steps to lower them if needed

## #6. Don't rely on the 20-20-20 rule

Look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds every 20 minutes. This is the 20-20-20 rule. It's a good guideline… but it's not a cure-all for digital eye strain.

What else helps:

- **screen position:** Position your computer screen ~4-5 inches below eye level, measured from the center of the screen.
- **longer breaks:** Take a 15+ min break after 2 hours of screen time.
- **blinking:** Blink rate can drop by ~70% when looking at a screen. Blink fully and deliberately to minimize your risk of dry eyes.

## What's Bryan doing?

Bryan is measuring 15 biomarkers important to eye health, including:

- osteoprotegerin
- osteopontin
- IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-17A, IL-17F
- TNF-α, MMP-9, TIMP-1, IL-10
- TGF-β, SOD, GDF-15, β-NGF

Two pieces of paper go into Bryan's eyeballs to absorb tear production, which we can use to quantify the molecular environment.** Things like active inflammation, tissue degradation, and regenerative signaling.

We'll then look at eye health protocols and use the results to track progress.

We'll share what we learn. In the meantime, the above protocols can help you protect your eyes and keep your vision sharp.

**Do not attempt to put pieces of paper into your eyeballs without the advice and supervision of a licensed ophthalmologist.

# 4 Mental Health Protocols

More than 90% of serotonin is produced in your gut. Not your brain.

Mood, motivation, emotional resilience… these are outputs of your biology. And biology responds to inputs you can control.

We reviewed the research on modifiable factors that affect mental health. Four mental health protocols stood out.

In this blog post:

- 4 physical factors that impact mental health
- what to do daily

## 4 physical factors that impact mental health

### #1. Eat plenty of fiber

Fiber is essential for gut health, and your gut affects your mental health.

The [gut microbiome](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/collections/daily-health-longevity/products/essential-microbiome) produces neuroactive compounds, like serotonin and dopamine-related metabolites, which can influence mood and motivation. Your gut also talks to your brain via a direct pathway known as the vagus nerve.

When the microbiome is disrupted, the consequences extend beyond digestion. The composition and abundance of gut microbiota are associated with several mental health disorders, including:

- anxiety
- depression
- bipolar disorder

On the flip side, better gut health is linked to better mental health.

Fiber, fruits, veggies, and whole grains may increase beneficial gut microbiota and reduce harmful microbiota, supporting mental health.

### #2. Avoid ultra-processed food

Higher ultra-processed food intake is associated with an increased risk of depression.

The good news: You can improve this.

Research shows people who reduced ultra-processed food intake by at least 3 servings a day had a lower risk of depression compared to those who did not reduce their intake.

### #3. Maintain a regular sleep schedule

[Sleep duration](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/blogs/news/10-habits-for-sleep) gets all the attention… but regularity may be just as important for mental health.

One study looked at sleep timing across 7 days and compared irregular sleepers to regular sleepers. Irregular sleepers were those whose sleep times shifted night to night, such as 10 pm to 6 am one night, then 2 am to 10 am the next.

Compared to irregular sleepers, regular sleepers had a 38% lower risk of depression and a 33% lower risk of anxiety.

Even if you get enough sleep, you still have a higher risk if that sleep is at irregular times.

There are a few possible reasons for this.

Irregular sleep can lead to:

- disrupted neurotransmitter mood-regulating systems
- compromised prefrontal cortex and emotion regulation
- systemic inflammation, which may be a pathway to mood disorders

### #4. Move your body

A study of over 1.2 million adults found that individuals who exercised reported ~43% fewer days of poor mental health in the past month compared to those who did not exercise.

The largest associations were seen from:

- 45 min of exercise per session
- exercising 3-5x a week
- cycling, team sports, and aerobic and gym activities (although all types of exercise were beneficial)

The mechanism is multi-layered. Exercise improves hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis function, which lowers the stress hormone cortisol. Your body also produces endorphins after exercise, which improves mood and reduces pain.

## Mental health protocols

- **what you eat:** Eat more fiber, fruits, veggies, whole grains, and [polyphenols](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/extra-virgin-olive-oil), all linked to better gut health and mental health. Minimize ultra-processed food.
- **when you sleep:** Go to bed and wake up at the same time each day (+/- 30 min). Stop eating 4+ hours before bed and wind down for 60 min before bed to fall asleep on time.
- **how you move:** Move daily, even just for 20 min. Aim for 3-5x workouts a week. Do what you enjoy… you're in luck if you like cycling.

Finally, mental health is not 1 thing. It is the sum of dozens of biological systems working together. There are lots of levers to pull.

Pick 1 lever to work on this week.

A 9°F (5°C) increase in nighttime temperature cuts sleep by an [average of 23 min](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12469264/), which adds up to 6 days of lost sleep over a year.

## Why is sleep temperature important?

### 1. Falling asleep

Your core body temperature needs to drop ~2-3°F (~1-1.5°C) to initiate sleep. Being too warm blocks that drop and may raise your heart rate before bed by 5 beats per minute.

The result: it takes you longer to fall asleep.

### 2. Deep sleep

The body wants to be at its lowest core temperature during deep sleep. This is the sleep stage when growth hormone is released, cellular repair happens, immune function is restored, and metabolic waste is cleared from the brain.

Heat exposure [decreases deep sleep](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3427038/) and increases wakefulness. 60-67°F maximizes deep sleep activity.

### 3. REM sleep

Your body stops regulating temperature during REM, making it entirely dependent on the environment. This is the stage for memory consolidation, emotional processing, and cognitive restoration.

You want 68-72°F. Too warm and REM gets cut short. Too cool and it's disrupted.

### 4. Waking up

Core temperature naturally rises in the early morning to prepare the body for wakefulness.

If you've had a hot, broken night of sleep, you'll wake up groggier than usual.

- **thermostat:** Set your bedroom temperature between 60-67°F (15-19°C).

# Lasers vs. LLLT for Hair Loss

They use LEDs while marketing themselves as laser therapy. These are not the same thing.

LLLT (low-level laser light therapy) is the gold standard for light-based hair loss treatments, according to the [American Hair Loss Association](https://www.americanhairloss.org/understanding-the-differences-between-red-light-therapy-led-caps-and-low-level-light-therapy-devices-for-hair-loss/). This blog post covers:

- what LLLT is and how it works
- how lasers differ from LEDs
- why we built the Blueprint laser cap
- what to look for in a device

## What is LLLT?

LLLT was discovered back in the 60s when physician Endre Mester noticed that laser light sped up hair regrowth in shaved mice.

It is now an FDA-cleared technology that can reverse hair loss, with visible results in ~4 months with 6 min of daily use.

## Laser vs. LED for hair loss

# PFAS: What Are They and How to Avoid Them

Bryan recently found forever chemicals (PFAS) in the artificial turf in his backyard.

PFAS are everywhere.

Skincare. Clothing. Cookware. Packaging. [97% of us](https://www.niehs.nih.gov/health/topics/agents/pfc) have them in our blood.

They may disrupt metabolism, lower fertility, and increase cancer risk.

In this blog post:

- what are PFAS
- where are they found
- how to avoid them

## What are PFAS?

PFAS (perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances) are a group of nearly 15,000 synthetic chemicals. They're used to make products non-stick and water-, stain-, and grease-resistant.

They break down extremely slowly, with some PFAS lasting thousands of years in the environment. Hence the nickname "forever chemicals."

PFAS can get into your blood, organs, and brain, and they're toxic at extremely low levels.

Exposure to PFAS has been linked to:

- developmental issues in children
- weakened immune system
- increased cholesterol levels
- obesity
- hormone disruption
- decreased fertility
- liver damage
- kidney, testicular, prostate, thyroid, and breast cancer

This might not be everything. We're still learning how some PFAS affect human health.

## Where are PFAS found?

PFAS can get into the soil, water, and air, and enter the food supply. You can be exposed to them by drinking water or eating food that's been contaminated with PFAS.

You can also find PFAS in:

- non-stick cooking pans
- food packaging, including fast food wrappers, pizza boxes, microwave popcorn bags, and grease-resistant paper (some PFAS packaging is being phased out in the U.S.)
- clothing, especially if it's water-resistant, stain-repellent, or dirt-repellent
- cosmetics, including skincare, haircare, make-up, and dental floss
- homeware, like furniture, bedding, and textiles if they're water- or stain-repellent

## How to avoid PFAS exposure

Start here:

- **use stainless steel, cast iron, or ceramic pans**. Avoid traditional PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) non-stick pans.
- **don't heat up food wrapped in plastic or grease-resistant packaging.**
- **check stain- or water-repellent clothing or homeware:** Some brands are PFAS-free.
- **test your drinking water:** Use filters if PFAS are high. Reverse osmosis systems and granular activated carbon can remove PFAS from water. (Boiling water doesn't remove PFAS and can actually increase the concentration.)
- **check cosmetic labels:** Avoid waterproof and long-lasting formulas, and ingredients like PTFE, perfluorononyl dimethicone, and trifluoroacetyl tripeptide-2. Blueprint [skincare](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/collections/skincare) and [haircare](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/collections/haircare) products are not formulated with added PFAS.
- **eat more fiber:** Fiber may help your body trap and excrete more PFAS. Get fiber from fruits, veggies, legumes, and whole grains. [Metabolic Protein](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/collections/metabolic-protein) has 8 grams of fiber if you need an easy way to increase your intake.

You can't always avoid PFAS in food or water… but there's a lot you can do to reduce your exposure from everyday products.

# How to Avoid Heavy Metals

Some heavy metals have a biological half-life of [16-30 years](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10537762/), meaning they can linger in the body for decades.

At high levels, they’re linked to cancer, heart disease, kidney damage… and many more bad things.

It’s easy to mistake the effects for normal aging: weaker bones, hearing loss, silent heart injury, higher stroke and diabetes risk.

The problem is, some foods and supplements contain dangerous levels of heavy metals. And many companies skip testing or don’t tell you what’s in their products.

In this blog post:

- what are heavy metals
- why they’re bad news
- how to avoid them

## What are heavy metals?

Heavy metals are naturally occurring metallic elements.

At low concentrations, some heavy metals (like zinc, iron, copper, and manganese) are essential for human health. At higher concentrations… they’re toxic.

Other heavy metals (like lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury) have no biological role and can also be toxic.

You can find heavy metals in:

- tap water
- foods, like fish, meat, dairy, cereals, and [chocolate](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/blogs/news/is-supermarket-chocolate-toxic)
- supplements, like creatine, fish oil, and protein powders
- tobacco smoke

## Dangers of heavy metals

Once inside your body, heavy metals can build up and interfere with antioxidant defenses and cellular processes. Harmful metals can also displace helpful metals, like calcium. This can cause damage to fats, proteins, and DNA.

Heavy metal exposure is linked to:

- lower sperm count
- diabetes
- neurological damage
- cardiovascular disease
- many types of cancer, including skin, bladder, kidney, thyroid, stomach, and lung cancer

## How to avoid heavy metals

### 1. Check your tap water

Tips:

- **find out if you have a lead service line:** This is the pipe running from the water main to your home. Contact your water utility or a licensed plumber to find out if it’s made of lead. Take extra precautions if it is, like using a filter certified to remove lead.
- **get your water tested for heavy metals:** Internal plumbing and faucets can also contain lead. Know what you’re working with and whether you need to replace faucets or upgrade filters.
- **use a water filter or reverse osmosis system:** Even if a filter can’t remove all heavy metals, it can help reduce your overall exposure.
- **flush pipes before drinking:** If you do *not* have a lead service line, flush for 30-45 seconds, or 1 min if you have old galvanized iron pipes. If you *do* have a lead service line, flush for 3-5 min. You can shower or do laundry to flush the service line. Then flush internal faucets for 30-45 seconds. Flush and fill up a container to store in the fridge to drink from throughout the day.

### 2. Check your food and supplements

Tips:

- if you eat fish, go for salmon, trout, and cod, which contain less mercury than tuna.
- rinse rice before cooking and drain after cooking to reduce arsenic. Rotate with other grains, like oats, quinoa, and barley.
- look for foods and supplements that have been third-party tested for heavy metals. Not all brands do this.

## Final thoughts on heavy metals

When we learned how dirty the mainstream food supply was, we started sourcing and testing our own foods. That’s how [Blueprint](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/) was born.

In the last year alone, we spent over $600,000 testing our ingredients.

Whether you’re buying from us or someone else, check for a third-party certificate of analysis (CoA) to know what you’re putting into your body. What gets in can stick around for decades.

- how to track

Before I dive in, it's important to note that facial aging is made up of *many* different parts.

Aging affects a lot…

- bone structure
- collagen
- hydration
- elasticity
- fat
- placement of tissue (gravity)

This blog post focuses on specific key facial aging *markers*, and it does not cover them all. So, I am not saying I look 21 years old… or that I am 21 years old according to *all* skin markers. Just the specific key skin markers that multi-spectral imaging can measure.

And according to those 8 markers, my skin age is 21 years old.

It's also worth noting that 5 years ago, I was eating McDonald's daily and did not do anything specific for my skin…

Then I met Bryan Johnson. We started our scientific health experiment together, and I started to change my core habits, which no doubt had a major impact on my overall aging.

Here's the earliest face scan I can find.

- at age 27, my skin was age 26.
- now age 30, my skin is age 21. (based on multispectral imaging measuring 8 skin markers)

This means that in 3 years, instead of *accumulating* 3 years of skin age, I reversed my skin age by 5 years.

## How does skin measurement work?

This device uses multispectral imaging. It uses standardized visible, polarized, and UV lighting to assess surface and subsurface skin features. It is a well-validated skin-analysis tool.

This measurement does a lot, but not everything.

**What it DOES measure:**

- spots
- pores
- wrinkles
- texture
- UV spots
- brown spots
- red areas
- porphyrins (bacterial byproducts, which highlight congestion)

**It does NOT measure:**

- collagen
- elasticity of skin
- structural bone
- plenty else

Currently, there's no easy way to measure things like collagen and bone loss.

## How do you start?

Do these 5 things:

1. Treat any major conditions

### #1 Treat diseases and conditions**

- acne
- rosacea
- eczema
- psoriasis
- actinic keratosis
- seborrheic dermatitis
- melasma

In my case, I had been struggling with acne for years. It was a horrible experience, but I didn't take it seriously.

I started microdosing Accutane and my life changed. (I do 40 mg a week under physician supervision.)

Each major condition has a different treatment plan. Chat with an LLM and your doctor, and follow a science-backed treatment path (not random marketing gimmicks).

### #2 Basic interventions

- avoid UV damage
- red light therapy

It's important that for each treatment you check what the potential risks are and make sure you're informed by your doctor (ideally a dermatologist).

Do this:

- sunscreen
- cover your skin when outside (hat, umbrella, face cloth, etc.)
- tint your car windows

### #5 Retest

Once you've tried a treatment, go back and rescan your face. Repeat this process, and watch your numbers change.

Skin is just like any other biological organ. You can:

- treat
- repeat

For women, this is especially important, because obviously beauty is a commodity that is sold to women, and most of the time the things they're selling don't work.

Knowing how to *measure* your skin is your best protection against this, for everyone.

I am about to become the female equivalent of Bryan Johnson.

# 4 Heart Health Protocols

Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death worldwide. Yet ~80% of cases are preventable.

We've got to fix that.

Lifestyle factors significantly influence your heart's health and biological age.

Bryan is proof. His blood pressure is lower than 90% of 18-year-olds and his vascular function is equivalent to that of someone in their late teens or early 20s.

That didn't happen overnight… it was through consistent daily habits.

In this blog post:

- the basics of heart health
- advanced protocols you might not think of

## The basics of heart health

To protect your heart and reduce your risk of cardiovascular disease:

- eat fruits, veggies, whole grains, nuts, seeds, lean proteins, and [extra virgin olive oil](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/collections/extra-virgin-olive-oil)
- eat fewer processed foods
- limit salt, added sugar, saturated fats, and alcohol
- exercise regularly
- get enough sleep
- avoid smoking
- maintain a healthy weight

## Advanced heart health protocols

Once you've mastered the basics above, you can expand your heart health protocol.

### #1. Light at night

Light exposure at night disrupts your circadian rhythm. This has downstream effects on your heart.

Short-term disruption causes an increase in heart rate, blood pressure, inflammation, blood clotting, and more. Circadian disruption also impairs glucose metabolism, increasing your risk of type 2 diabetes, a risk factor for heart disease.

One study found people who got more light exposure at night had a higher risk of:

- coronary artery disease
- heart attack
- heart failure
- stroke

This was true even after adjusting for cardiovascular risk factors like diet, exercise, smoking, alcohol, and sleep duration.

**What to do:**

- dim the lights 1-2 hours before bed.
- avoid blue light and use red or amber light instead.
- use blackout blinds, curtains, or an eyemask.

### #2. Social connection

Social connection could affect longevity as much as exercise and obesity.

When lonely or socially isolated, you're more likely to engage in unhealthy behaviors, like smoking and being sedentary. Your immune system goes down, and your blood pressure goes up.

The effect is surprisingly large. Poor social relationships are associated with a ~30% increased risk of coronary heart disease and stroke.

**What to do:**

- set up weekly recurring social plans (consistency compounds).
- aim for 1 meaningful conversation a day.
- schedule time with friends as you would work meetings.

### #3. Sauna

Your heart rate increases during a sauna session, mimicking a low-to-moderate intensity workout. This can improve blood pressure and left ventricular function (the side that pumps blood from your heart to the rest of your body).

Regular sauna use may reduce your risk of:

- sudden cardiac death
- fatal coronary heart disease
- fatal cardiovascular disease

The more often you sauna, the better.

| Sauna frequency | Coronary heart disease risk | Cardiovascular disease risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2-3x/week | 23% lower | 27% lower |
| 4-7x/week | 48% lower | 50% lower |

Longer sessions (11-19 min) are also more beneficial for heart health than shorter sessions (<11 min).

**What to do:**

- if you have access to a sauna, use it.
- aim for 176-212°F (80-100°C), 15-20 min, 3-5x a week if you're getting started.

**What Bryan does:**

- 200°F (93°C)
- 20 min daily
- ice pack on the boys to protect fertility markers
- wool hat or towel to protect scalp
- [Blueprint SFC Facial Moisturizer](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/collections/skincare) before sauna, and a face mask and [Blueprint SFC Facial Serum](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/collections/skincare) a few times a week after sauna to prevent skin drying

[See Bryan's latest sauna protocol here.](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/blogs/news/sauna-protocol)

**Skip sauna sessions if you:**

- have serious heart issues or uncontrolled blood pressure
- are pregnant (consult your doctor)
- have an infection, fever, or feel unwell
- have a history of seizures
- struggle with respiratory conditions (asthma, COPD)
- have irritated or inflamed skin
- recently consumed alcohol or recreational drugs
- are taking medications such as beta-blockers, stimulants, anticholinergics, or diuretics

### #4. Monitoring biomarkers

Monitor your:

- blood pressure
- cholesterol
- blood sugar
- apolipoprotein B (ApoB)

High blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar are all risk factors for heart attacks and stroke. You might not know you have high levels until it's too late.

High blood pressure, in particular, is a silent killer. There are often no symptoms, yet it is one of the biggest causes of heart attack and stroke.

ApoB carries bad-for-you fats, like cholesterol, around your body. High levels are associated with an increased risk of heart attack and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (a build-up of fats and plaque in your arteries).

**What to do:**

- get a blood pressure cuff to monitor blood pressure at home.
- test cholesterol, blood sugar, and ApoB regularly (you can test through [Biomarkers](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/pages/biomarkers)).
- if your numbers are concerning, make lifestyle changes (like diet, exercise, and sleep) to work toward healthier ranges.

There is a lot you can do to protect your heart. Start with the foundations: diet, exercise, sleep. Layer additional protocols from there.

# Should You Take Olive Oil Shots?

Morning olive oil shots are suddenly all over the internet.

Kourtney Kardashian does it. Ryan Seacrest does it. Hailey Bieber does it with lemon juice.

Is this another wellness fad, or is there legit science behind it? It depends on the quality of your olive oil...

In this blog post:

- why "extra virgin" is important
- longevity benefits
- what about lemon juice?
- what to look for in an olive oil

## What is EVOO?

Extra virgin olive oil (EVOO) is the highest-quality grade an olive oil can get. The ranking is: olive oil < virgin olive oil < extra virgin olive oil.

Virgin and extra virgin olive oils must be:

- extracted by mechanical means (not via heat or chemicals)
- produced without heat or chemical solvents
- evaluated using chemical analysis and a panel of taste testers

Extra virgin olive oil must then:

- be free of taste and smell defects
- have positive fruity characteristics
- have a free acidity of 0.8% or lower

## Longevity benefits of olive oil

Olive oil has a high concentration of monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) and polyphenols.

A diet low in saturated fats with a high concentration of MUFAs, like oleic acid, promotes cardiovascular health and a healthy inflammatory response.

Polyphenols have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, and may increase high-density lipoprotein (good cholesterol) and promote endothelial (blood vessel lining) function.

EVOO may also support cognition, gut health, and cell maintenance.

In short: It's a longevity food you want in your diet.

*Note: Olive oil is calorie dense. To get the possible heart health benefits, swap it for other fats in your diet to account for the extra calories.*

### Should you consume it in the morning?

Some claim taking a morning shot of olive oil on an empty stomach increases the health benefits. There's no research backing that up.

From what we know so far, timing and food pairing don't matter. What matters is that it's a part of your protocol.

### What about with lemon juice?

Lemon juice contains vitamin C, which has antioxidant effects and plays a role in immune function and iron absorption. But there's little research on combining olive oil with lemon juice.

If you like the taste, go for it. But it's more important to add olive oil to your diet, with or without lemon.

## What to look for in an olive oil

Purity, freshness, and polyphenol content are all important for olive oil's health benefits.

Look for:

- extra virgin (not virgin or just olive oil)
- cold pressed (made without heat or chemical solvents)
- high polyphenol count (>400mg/kg)
- high oleic acid count (>67%)
- recent harvest date (fresher olives = more nutrients)

You also want a peppery taste. Polyphenols are responsible for the strong taste and dry mouthfeel of EVOO. More taste = more polyphenol health benefits.

[Blueprint EVOO](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/collections/extra-virgin-olive-oil) is all of the above. It's also:

- harvested from alternating hemispheres for maximum freshness
- third-party tested for purity and heavy metals
- stored in UV-protected glass to maintain integrity

## How to consume olive oil

Consume 1-3 tablespoons of high-quality EVOO per day. This can be as a morning shot or drizzled on salads, veggies, or mixed into a protein shake.

Bryan consumes 3 tablespoons of [Blueprint EVOO](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/collections/extra-virgin-olive-oil) daily.

# Is HBOT Worth the Hype?

Written by Bryan Johnson • 02.20.2026

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) ranks as one of the highest value health therapies I've done.

Here's:

- the science behind HBOT
- my protocol
- my biomarkers after 60 sessions
- what to do if you can't do HBOT

## The science behind HBOT

HBOT involves breathing pure oxygen (100%) in a pressurized chamber at anything above atmospheric pressure (2 ATA, atmospheres absolute, is equivalent to being 33 feet under seawater).

The increased pressure enhances the lungs' ability to absorb oxygen, boosting oxygen levels throughout the body. The therapy aims to promote rejuvenation by increasing oxygen concentration in tissues, supporting healing, cellular repair, and vascularization (the growth of blood vessels).

## HBOT is used for recovery and rehabilitation

HBOT is clinically used for:

- treating carbon monoxide poisoning
- supporting chronic wounds with some success in diabetics
- recovery of radiation injuries
- supporting recovery from sports injuries

## HBOT is promising for rejuvenation and longevity

A landmark clinical trial showed evidence of HBOT increasing telomere length in a small cohort of healthy older adults (age >64 years).

Increases in telomere length of 20-38% were demonstrated in multiple types of circulating immune cells. The effect was also sustained 1-2 weeks after ending the HBOT protocol.

The study also found a significant decrease in the fraction of senescent (aged) T-cells at the end of the protocol.

This finding is significant for longevity because telomere length decreases with age and is an important marker of biological age.

In two randomized clinical trials, HBOT also improved physical performance in mid-aged elite athletes (age 40-50), as well as in healthy older adults (age >64). In both cases, the observed improvements included an increase in VO2 max, a key marker for health and longevity.

A preclinical and clinical study in an Alzheimer's mouse model and in 6 elderly Alzheimer patients (age >64) showed HBOT improved vascular function and cognitive performance, and reduced amyloid (a protein) burden in the brain.

## My HBOT protocol

- hard shell chamber
- 2 ATA
- 90-min sessions
- 20 min breathing 100% oxygen, 5-min break, repeat
- 5 sessions per week, 2 days off
- 60 sessions within 90 days

Inside my chamber, the oxygen level is 21%, which is the same as Earth's atmosphere. Other chambers maintain 100% oxygen inside, creating increased fire risk.

The 100% oxygen is delivered through a mask.

Important: do not take any electronics into the chamber as it creates a fire risk.

## Results from 60 sessions of HBOT

- wiped out detectable systemic inflammation in my body
- 300% increase in VEGF (formation of new blood vessels)
- telomerase activity of a 12-year-old, associated with biological age
- 250% and 290% increase in short-chain fatty acids and n-butyrate, respectively, important microbiome markers
- complete elimination of metabolic imbalance in my gut
- 28.6% reduction in a dementia marker
- improved muscle oxygenation
- dramatic improvements to whole-body skin health

After achieving elite-level biomarkers over the past 4+ years, my team and I have struggled to find new therapies that meaningfully improve my biomarkers.

HBOT achieved that.

### Inflammation

Chronic inflammation is the foundation of disease and all things bad health. Before HBOT, my inflammation markers were in the top 5% of 18-29-year-olds (you get more inflamed as you age).

HBOT lowered my systemic inflammation to below detection limits.

This is wild.

A second test to confirm the inflammation measurement (my CRPm, an epigenetic biomarker proxy for inflammation) is in the lowest 1%.

### Vascularization

300% increase in VEGF.

VEGF drives the formation of new blood vessels, improving tissue perfusion and oxygenation, which are essential for improving fitness and physical and cognitive performance. It also has further pro-longevity effects on gene expression.

HBOT improved muscle oxygenation, which reached the same level of exercise power (wattage) at more than double the muscle oxygenation.

### Telomeres

I now have the telomerase activity of a 12-year-old (7.7%).

Telomeres keep chromosomes from falling apart. They are essential for healthy cell division, including stem cell renewal. As we age, cells lose their telomerase activity and telomeres get shorter. When telomeres are too short, cells may become senescent (aged) and contribute to accelerated aging.

### Microbiome

We saw dramatic improvements in my microbiome.

A high metabolic imbalance score might be indicative of a lack of pre-biotics in the diet (including fiber). Interestingly in my case, HBOT was enough to reverse the metabolic imbalance despite no significant change in my diet.

### Brain health

28.6% reduction in the brain damage and dementia marker pTau217.

| Timing | pTau217 |
| --- | --- |
| Pre-HBOT | 0.14 pg/mL |
| Post-HBOT | 0.1 pg/mL |

The phosphoprotein pTau217 is a specific marker associated with Alzheimer's disease.

Levels higher than 0.18 pg/mL are potentially indicative of plaque accumulation in the brain. Keeping this marker at the lowest end is a great relief and a sign of improved brain health.

Lower pTau217 is associated with lower tau pathology and is linked to better preservation of:

- memory
- processing speed
- executive function
- neuronal stability

### Skin

| Timing | Facial skin age | UV spots score |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-HBOT | 39 years old | 55th percentile |
| Post-HBOT | 38 years old | 68th percentile |

This is indicative of significant removal of advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) from the skin, perhaps due to improved vascularization.

Subjectively, I've never seen a more dramatic improvement in my skin quality than from these 60 HBOT sessions.

## Free or low-cost alternatives to HBOT

HBOT can be expensive. Here are some free or low-cost activities you can do to get some of the same effects…

- **sauna:** Linked to a reduction in systemic inflammation and pTau217.
- **sleep:** Sleep loss is linked to shorter telomeres in men, and it increases tau-related neurodegenerative signaling (bad for long-term brain health).
- **exercise:** Linked to reduction in systemic inflammation and increases VEGF.
- **nutrition:** The Mediterranean (Blueprint) diet is linked to longer telomeres and higher telomerase activity. It also increases gut microbiota diversity.
- **meditation:** Meditation is linked to longer telomeres, especially in women.
- **smart UV exposure:** Chronic UV exposure causes 80-90% of visible facial aging.

Want to do HBOT, but don't know where?

Soon, you will be able to find clinics and health practitioners that are Don't Die Certified, meaning they follow the same scientific rigor and measurement as my protocol.

# The Three Power Laws of Health

# The Three Power Laws of Health

Written by Bryan Johnson • 04.04.2025

Hi Friend,

Today is World Health Day.

I want to share something simple, but powerful: the 3 Power Laws of health.

****If you do these three things, you will:

Have more energy.
Think more clearly.
Sleep better.

Let’s begin.

**Power Law 1: Sleep**

**Reframe your identity.**
You are no longer someone who tries to get better sleep.
You are a **professional sleeper.**

That means you don’t sleep when it’s convenient. You don’t sleep after your show ends, or after finishing up some late-night emails, or after one more scroll through social media.

**Treat sleep as a craft, something you continually improve****.** It’s the foundation of every other part of your life. If you get your sleep right, everything else becomes easier.

Here are 5 things to do immediately:

**1. Eat earlier. Eat lighter.**

If your bedtime is 10 p.m., have your last meal by 8 p.m. Then push it to 7. Then try 6. Then 5.

Find what works for you.

You will quickly learn: **the earlier and lighter you eat, the better you'll sleep.**

**2. Build a wind-down routine.**

Your body can’t go from hyper-focused work or buzzing social energy straight into sleep mode. It needs a transitional wind down phase.

One hour before bed, shift your state. Screens off. No scrolling.

Turn to breathwork, meditation, reading, stretching, or a walk. You’re sending your nervous system a signal: it’s time to slow down.

**3. Adjust your lighting.**

Bright white lights signal alertness.

If you want to fall asleep fast, switch to **red light** in the evening.

I’ve replaced lamps in my house with red bulbs. They’re incredibly effective. The mood calms. Everyone winds down.

**4. Stick to your bedtime.**

Routine is everything.

If your bedtime is 10 p.m., aim to go to bed within 30 minutes of that every night.

Deviate, and your body gets confused. Sleep quality suffers.

Even with the same number of hours, inconsistent timing reduces sleep efficiency and recovery.

******5. Avoid stimulants.**

This one is obvious but easy to overlook.

If you're going to bed at 10 p.m., be mindful of your caffeine intake. Caffeine has a half-life of ~6 hours. A cup of coffee at 4 pm means that half a cup of coffee is in your system at 10 pm. Don’t let a badly timed coffee ruin your night.

**Power Law 2: Exercise**

When you sleep **well**, you feel **well.**
When you feel **well**, you move **well**.
And when you **move**, you feel even **better**.

**That’s the loop we’re building.**

**Start here:**

1.

**Move your body for 30 minutes a day**. This could be walking, running, swimming, strength training, biking. Anything that gets your heart rate up.

2.

**Break up your day with movement**. Every 20 - 30 minutes, get up. I do this constantly: stretch, take a few steps, reset.

Moving your body throughout the day is just as important as your structured workouts.

From here, you can go deeper. There’s an infinite rabbit hole of protocols, programs, and progressions.

**But the basics are the basics:**

Be active every day. Move every hour or so.

Your body craves movement. Give it what it needs.

**Power Law 3: Diet**

Now, this one’s complicated. Because food is emotional.
We use it to **self-soothe**.
We use it to **celebrate**.
We use it when we feel stuck.

I know this firsthand. I was trapped. If you're struggling here, I see you.

**That’s why diet is Power Law #3**, not #1. When you're well-rested and moving, you naturally want to eat better.

If you're sleep-deprived and sedentary, your cravings take over.

So here’s the truth:

**1. Never rely on willpower.**

If there’s a time of day you always cave, for example, 7 p.m. that may include cookies or other late-night snacks, you can use a system for strength instead of willpower.

Don’t wait until you're in the danger zone to decide. Decide ahead of time.

You’re someone who doesn’t eat cookies at 7 p.m. Period. Make it a rule. Not a debate.

**2. Fire your worst self.**

For me, it was Evening Bryan.
From 5 p.m. to 10 p.m., he was guaranteed to overeat. Every single day.

So I fired him.

**I made a rule**: no food after 5 p.m.
It wasn’t about self-control. It was about self-preservation.
You might not need that exact rule. But you probably know which version of you needs to be fired.
**
3. Eat the [Don’t Die Food Guide](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/pages/blueprint-protocol#eat)..**

Healthy fats. Quality proteins. Lots of plants.

It’s not about being perfect. It’s about being directionally correct, consistently.

Follow the Don’t Die Food Guide [here](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/pages/blueprint-protocol#eat).

**4. Avoid the obvious traps.**

Too much sugar. Too much alcohol. Smoking. You know what they are.

You don’t need me to tell you. But you do need to decide where your standards are. And stick to them.

We live in a world where personal health is insanely hard. I know; I’ve felt hopeless and helpless too.

**But now, I have systems.**

If you’re reading this right now, eating junk food, feeling off track, that’s okay.
You’re here. You’re trying. That’s what matters.

[We’re building a community for a new societal norm of health](https://dontdieapp.com/).
Where being healthy is normal.
Where we support each other in the micro-moments.

So when you’re about to give in, don’t just think about yourself.

**Do it for everyone else.**

Because when you make the right choice, others will too. And when you cave, we all feel it.

**Final word:**

You don’t need to be perfect. You need to be committed.

These 3 Power Laws are your foundation.
Master them, and you’ll become the happiest, healthiest version of yourself.

Then we can start playing with all the cool stuff on top.

But first:

Don’t do it. I’m telling you. Don’t cave. Not tonight.

Be well,

Bryan

When I started Blueprint, people didn’t know what category to place me so they’d blurt out words like vampire, Patrick Bateman, techbro, f*#@ face, biohacker, Prometheus, Dorian Grey, and more.

Understanding rejuvenation as a sport helps confer some respect and formality to the practice. With this framework, I created the Rejuvenation Olympics.

A leaderboard for people who want to compete on their speed of aging, or rather the slowness thereof.

I was doing two things with this.

First, up until I started [Project Blueprint](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/) and [Don’t Die](https://dontdie.com/), health influencers and health fads were primarily storytelling-based and anecdotal. **What was missing: rigorous science, measurement and data.**
